source.title: On the Nonlinearity of Layer Normalization
source.authors: Yun-Hao Ni; Yu-Xin Guo; Junlong Jia; Lei Huang

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation affecting the extracted results.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains linear-plus-layer-normalization networks on random labels and measures training accuracy, directly addressing random-label fitting. Its networks and normalization variants differ from the standard deep networks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports random-label training accuracy for LN-Net and LN-Net with group-based LN (LN-G). It does not report random-label test error. Random-label results cited from Zhang et al. are prior work and are not extracted as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study measures random-label training accuracy after gradient-based training of nonlinear LN networks, bearing on V1's fitting component in a specialized architecture. It searches training configurations rather than testing unchanged standard architectures and hyperparameters. Purely linear controls do not test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the empirical capacity argument, but should foreground the theoretical result: LN alone supplies nonlinearity and LN-Net can represent arbitrary finite label assignments; suitable grouping strengthens empirical capacity. The authors claim perfect random-label fitting on both datasets, but Table IV reports a maximum of only 95.96% on MNIST-RL, versus 100% on CIFAR-10-RL. They also acknowledge that practical LN-G evidence is limited to small networks and datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the random-label fitting approach attributed to Zhang et al. (2017), but evaluates linear-plus-LN networks and LN-G variants rather than standard deep networks; it also searches hyperparameters and reports best accuracies.
record.method_sensitivity: Training accuracy varies with network depth, group count, and dataset. The authors report particularly poor performance at group number 128, where each group has two neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructive proofs establish that width-three LN networks with O(m) normalization layers can classify m distinct samples with arbitrary labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LN networks have sufficient representational capacity for arbitrary finite label assignments; this does not establish that stochastic gradient training finds those parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Hessian-based nonlinearity increases with suitable group partitioning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grouping can amplify LN's measured nonlinearity; this measure alone does not establish random-label fitting.

record.problems: The random-label experiments report training accuracy only, not test error. The tested LN-Net is a specialized network without activation functions, and LN-G changes the normalization. The authors report best results from hyperparameter configurations; the reported random-label experiments use a fixed random seed for LN-Net and LN-G.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining per-depth and group-count combinations in Appendix F.1.3 Tables III and IV were omitted to stay within 60 rows. Included baseline LN-Net depth results, perfect CIFAR-10-RL cases, MNIST-RL LN-G group-32 cases, and poor group-128 cases to retain incomplete, successful, and outcome-changing conditions.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error, standard architectures with unchanged training hyperparameters, and a matched true-label training comparison. Results are selected over optimizer or learning-rate configurations, using a fixed seed for the neural networks.
Training-time ratio between true and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Empirical fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test errors across a label-corruption sweep; remaining-signal capture while memorizing noise.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing those regularizers.
Learning real patterns before noise and comparisons of real-label versus random-label learning trajectories.

missing.what: The BN replacement experiment reportedly fails to exceed the linear-classifier bound on both random-label datasets. Add the qualitative result, with numerical accuracy and training details marked unavailable.
missing.locator: Section 5.2, Verify the Nonlinearity of LN, paragraph on Batch Normalization
missing.versions: V1 fitting component in another specialized normalization-only architecture

record.verdict_notes: V1 links concern its random-label fitting component in an architectural extension. The results do not directly refute the original claim about standard networks under unchanged hyperparameters. All tabulated network accuracies are selected training outcomes, not replicated estimates; uncertainty is not reported. Omitted group/depth combinations are already declared in rows_left_out and are therefore not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label training accuracy is measured, but random-label test error at chance is not reported. The study does not test standard networks with their original architectures and hyperparameters: its LN-Net has no activation functions, and LN-G changes the normalization.

source_check.notes:
Internal discrepancies: Section 5.2 gives 55.85% versus Table II's 55.58%, and claims perfect MNIST-RL fitting despite Table IV's maximum 95.96%.
The experiments report selected training accuracies; chance test error and unchanged true-label hyperparameters are untested.
